newsitem.title: USA: Huge campaign gifts raise questions in U.S.election.
newsitem.headline: Huge campaign gifts raise questions in U.S.election.

text.p: Mickey Mouse does it. Archer Daniels Midland, the soybean king, does it. A Cuban drug dealer did it so well he was invited to the White House. Even an impoverished Buddhist nun is getting into the act.

While millions of ordinary Americans think all one has to to do to keep democracy going is vote, corporations, special interests and foreigners are finding that you can also perform a service by donating lots of money to the party of your choice, or maybe even both parties.

Even though rules have been tightened over individual campaign contributions, true campaign finance reform has lagged. One result is that contributors are delivering record amounts of cash through loopholes in the laws. Another is an ugly scandal over whether candidates and the U.S. electoral system are up for sale as the presidential election heads into its last days.

Tobacco companies Philip Morris and RJR Nabisco together gave the Republican Party more than $2 million up to the start of the summer. Meanwhile, Mickey Mouse's boss, the Walt Disney Co., gave the Democratic party $532,000, joining such Hollywood salwarts as MCA Inc. and Dream Works SKG in trying to keep that party's dream alive.
Archer Daniels Midland, one of many companies to donate to both parties, gave $335,000 to the Republicans and $110,000 to the Democrats.
And their contributions are not alone.

In recent weeks, President Bill Clinton's Democratic party has been hit with scandals involving contributions from an Indonesian banking family, a Korean business, a Cuban drug kingpin and $325,000 from a man named Yogesh K. Ghandi, who also wanted to give the president a peace prize.
A Democratic party fundraiser with Indonesian connections, John Huang, is in hiding while a federal judge wants to talk to him.

Meanwhile Vice President Al Gore is trying to figure out how his visit to a Buddhist temple near Los Angeles for a little meditation turned into a $140,000 fundraiser where the Wall Street Journal reported an impoverished nun was given $5,000 to hand over as a contribution.
And many others are trying to figure out how Jorge Cabrera, a reputed Cuban-American drug kingpin, wound up at the White House for a reception after donating $20,000.
Among the puzzled are billionaire Ross Perot, the independent presidential candidate who thinks political contributions should begin and end at home.

"I never thought I would live to see a major drug dealer give 20,000 bucks ... and then be invited to the White House for a reception. Now keep in mind, you can't get into the White House unless the Secret Service clears you," Perot said in a speech on Thursday at the National Press Club.

"This guy had been convicted, arrested twice in the '80s, it's in the computer. Forrest Gump ... would have picked that up, right? But every now and then the White House just overrule them, say let them in anyhow."
Perot warned that Clinton's looseness in accepting questionable contributions, among other scandals, could be devastating if he wins a second term.
"We are headed toward a second Watergate with all this stuff going on and a constitutional crisis in 1997. Just remember where you heard it and put it in the bank," he said.

Political contributions from businesses, unions and a myriad of special interests are nothing new in American politics, and are routinely denounced as a system of legally sanctioned bribery that skewers the political system.
But the amounts given this year have been staggering both for their size and boldness in a year when public funding of the presidential campaigns was supposed to help block excesses.
Besides giving individual contributions of up to $20,000, contributors have found a loophole -- direct donations to the political parties for "party building work."

The Centre for Responsive Politics, which tracks contributions, says up that up to June 30 more than $155 million has been contributed to the two parties through what is called "the soft money loophole" as compared to $80 million during the 1992 presidential election.
